chapter.name: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures

questions.q:
Rhea's mother makes poha with flattened rice, peanuts, curry leaves, chopped onion and a squeeze of lemon.
(a) Is the poha a uniform or a non-uniform mixture? Give the observation that decides it.
(b) Rhea stirs the poha for five more minutes and says it has now become a uniform mixture. Using your answer to (a), explain whether extra stirring can change its type.
questions.a: (a) Non-uniform: the peanuts, curry leaves, onion and rice can be told apart with the naked eye. (b) No. Stirring only spreads the pieces around; the peanuts, leaves and onion pieces can still be seen separately, which is the test used in (a), so the poha stays non-uniform.
s: (a) non-uniform, because the components are visible with the naked eye
(b) stirring does not make the components invisible, so it stays non-uniform

questions.q: Kiran stirs a spoon of sugar into a glass of water until no grains are left. Under the school microscope a drop shows no separate sugar, yet the water tastes sweet. Which description of the sweet water is correct?
questions.a: A uniform mixture in which sugar keeps its taste
o: A uniform mixture in which sugar keeps its taste
A new substance, since the sugar can no longer be seen
A non-uniform mixture, since two things were stirred
A pure substance, since it looks the same throughout

questions.q: Swati says, 'Air helps things burn, so every gas in air must take part in combustion.' Which fact from the chapter shows that her reasoning is wrong?
questions.a: Nitrogen (about 78%) does not take part in combustion
o: Nitrogen (about 78%) does not take part in combustion
Oxygen is needed by most living beings to stay alive
Air is a uniform mixture, so its gases cannot be seen apart
Carbon dioxide in the air turns lime water milky

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Nagpur left a dish of clear lime water open on a window sill and wrote this record under their teacher's supervision.
9 a.m.: lime water clear and colourless.
1 p.m.: lime water milky; a thin white layer at the bottom.
Conclusion 1: Air contains carbon dioxide.
Conclusion 2: The white layer is dust that fell into the dish from the air.
A second dish of the same lime water, filled to the brim and tightly closed, stayed clear all day.
(a) What does the milkiness show, and which substance in air caused it?
(b) Find the error in Conclusion 2 and correct it.
(c) Explain why the closed dish stayed clear.
(d) The group wants to add a third conclusion. Decide which ONE of these the record supports, and explain why the other cannot be drawn from it: 'Carbon dioxide is present in the air by the window' or 'The air by the window has more carbon dioxide than the air in the classroom'.
questions.a: (a) It shows carbon dioxide is present in the air; the carbon dioxide reacted with the calcium hydroxide in the lime water. (b) The white layer is not dust: it is calcium carbonate, tiny insoluble white particles formed when carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide (calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide gives calcium carbonate + water). (c) The closed, full dish had no air touching the lime water, so no carbon dioxide could reach it and no calcium carbonate formed. (d) Only 'Carbon dioxide is present in the air by the window'. The milkiness shows that carbon dioxide reached the lime water, so it is present. The second conclusion compares two places, but the group tested only the window sill; with no dish in the classroom there is nothing to compare, so the record cannot show which air has more.
s: (a) carbon dioxide in air reacts with the lime water
(b) the white layer is calcium carbonate formed by the reaction, not dust
(c) no air, so no carbon dioxide, reached the closed dish
(d) supports presence only; no classroom dish, so no comparison can be made

Statement 1: A sprout salad is non-uniform because its green gram, chickpeas, onion and tomato can be seen with the naked eye.
Statement 2: A mixture of black and yellow powders in which both colours can still be seen becomes uniform once it is stirred well.
Statement 3: In sugar water the sugar keeps its own property of sweetness.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Dhruv collected air on black paper sheets at his school in Kanpur on five different days, and every sheet caught some dust. He says, 'Dust is a component of air, just like nitrogen and oxygen, because it is always there.' Do you agree? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. (1) The chapter says dust particles are only suspended in the air; they are not an integral part of air and are considered pollutants. (2) The nature and the number of dust particles vary from time to time and from place to place, so dust is not a fixed part of the air the way its gases are. Finding dust on five days in one place shows that the air there carried dust on those days, not that dust belongs to air.
s: verdict: disagree
dust is suspended in air and is a pollutant, not an integral part
the amount and kind of dust vary with time and place

questions.q:
A science teacher in Indore gives her class three spice-shelf samples and these observations.
M1: mustard seeds mixed with cumin seeds - both kinds of seed seen with the naked eye.
M2: very fine turmeric powder mixed with very fine red chilli powder - looks an even orange to the naked eye; under a magnifying glass, yellow grains and red grains can be told apart.
M3: glucose stirred into water - nothing seen separately, even under a microscope.
(a) Classify M1, M2 and M3 as uniform or non-uniform, quoting the observation that decides each. (3)
(b) Explain, using M2, why the chapter's test for a non-uniform mixture allows a magnifying device and not only the naked eye. (1)
(c) A fourth jar, M4, is described only as 'looks the same throughout to the naked eye'. Explain why this is not enough to classify M4, and what further observation would settle it. (1)
questions.a: (a) M1 non-uniform: its components are visible with the naked eye. M2 non-uniform: its components can be told apart with a magnifying glass, a magnifying device. M3 uniform: its components cannot be distinguished even under a microscope. (b) M2 looks even to the naked eye, yet it is not evenly mixed at the level of its grains; a magnifying device reveals the separate components, so judging by the naked eye alone would wrongly call it uniform. (c) Like M2, a mixture can look the same to the naked eye and still have components that a magnifying device shows. M4 must be examined with a magnifying glass and, if nothing is seen, with a microscope: components seen means non-uniform; nothing seen even under a microscope means uniform.
s: (a) M1 non-uniform, M2 non-uniform, M3 uniform, each with its deciding observation
(b) M2 shows a naked-eye judgement can miss components that a magnifying device reveals
(c) the naked eye is not enough; examine with a magnifier and a microscope

questions.q: A balloon is filled with 2,500 mL of air. Taking nitrogen as 78% of air, the balloon holds ___ mL of the gas in air that does not take part in combustion and makes up most of it.

On a humid afternoon in Chennai, a steel tumbler of iced water left on a table becomes wet on the outside, though it is not leaking.
(a) Where does the water on the outside come from?
(b) What does this show about air? Explain also what this shows about air, and why this component could not be seen in the air before it reached the tumbler.
questions.a: (a) From the water vapour in the air: when warm air touches the cool surface, the water vapour turns into tiny droplets of liquid water. (b) It shows that water vapour is one of the components of air. Air is a uniform mixture, so its components are evenly distributed and cannot be told apart; the vapour becomes visible only after it turns into liquid droplets.
s: (a) water vapour in air turns into droplets on the cool surface
(b) water vapour is a component of air; in a uniform mixture it cannot be seen separately

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Stainless steel is called a uniform mixture.
Reason (R): The iron, nickel, chromium and carbon in stainless steel do not react chemically with each other.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Kabir places a bowl of sprout salad and a glass of sugar water side by side. In which way are the two alike?
questions.a: In both, each component keeps its properties
o: In both, each component keeps its properties
In both, the components are spread evenly
In both, the components can be told apart
In both, the components have reacted together

questions.q: True or false? 'Air cannot be a mixture, because it looks the same everywhere and none of its gases can be seen separately.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Looking the same throughout is the mark of a uniform mixture, not of a single substance. Air is a uniform mixture of mainly nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and its components keep their own properties: oxygen helps combustion while nitrogen does not take part in it.
s: verdict: false
air is a uniform mixture; its components keep their own properties though they cannot be seen apart

questions.q: A rangoli powder looks a single pink colour from a distance, but under a magnifying glass red and white grains can be told apart. How should the powder be classified?
questions.a: Non-uniform, as a magnifier shows its components
o: Non-uniform, as a magnifier shows its components
Uniform, as it looks one colour to the naked eye
Uniform, as the grains are too fine to pick out by hand
Non-uniform only if a microscope also shows the grains

questions.q:
Air and stainless steel are very different to look at and touch, yet the chapter classes both the same way.
(i) State the class of matter both belong to, and the observation that puts them there. (1)
(ii) Name the components of each. (1)
(iii) Explain why neither can be called a pure substance in science, although each looks the same throughout. (1)
questions.a: (i) Both are uniform mixtures: their components are evenly distributed and cannot be seen separately, even under a microscope. (ii) Air: mainly nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. Stainless steel: iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon. (iii) Each contains more than one substance, so it has more than one type of particle; a pure substance has no other substance present in it. Looking the same throughout shows only that the mixture is uniform.
s: (i) both uniform mixtures, components not distinguishable
(ii) components of air and of stainless steel
(iii) more than one substance, so not pure; uniform look does not mean pure

questions.q:
Match each observation with what it shows.
Column A:
1. A drop of sugar water under a microscope shows nothing separate
2. A steel tumbler of iced water gets wet on the outside
3. A black sheet near an open window collects tiny specks
4. Lime water left in an open dish turns milky
Column B:
a. Carbon dioxide is present in air
b. Water vapour is present in air
c. Dust is suspended in air
d. The mixture is uniform

A shopkeeper in Lucknow says his 'mixed dry fruit' of almonds, cashews and raisins is a uniform mixture because every packet holds exactly the same weight of each.
(a) Classify the dry fruit using the observation the chapter uses to decide, and say what is wrong with his reason.
(b) He then grinds a packet into a fine powder that looks the same all over, even through a magnifying glass. What further observation is needed before it can be called uniform?
questions.a: (a) Non-uniform: the almonds, cashews and raisins are easily seen apart with the naked eye. Equal weights in every packet are not what 'uniform' means; the chapter decides by whether the components can be seen separately. (b) It must be examined under a microscope. Only if the components cannot be distinguished even under a microscope is it uniform; if separate kinds of particle are seen there, it is still non-uniform.
s: (a) non-uniform by visibility; equal weights do not decide
(b) a microscope check: uniform only if nothing separate is seen even then

questions.q:
Meena runs a juice stall in Pune and sells two drinks. Clear nimbu pani is lemon juice, sugar, salt and water stirred until nothing can be seen separately, even under a microscope at the school lab. Masala nimbu pani is the same clear drink with mint leaves and roasted cumin seeds floating in it. A customer asks Meena for 'the drink in which the ingredients have not changed into something new'.
(a) Classify each drink as uniform or non-uniform with the observation that decides it.
(b) Meena leaves a glass of clear nimbu pani in the sun until all the water has gone. A white crust remains that tastes both sweet and salty. Explain what this shows about the sugar and salt in the drink.
(c) Using (a) and (b), decide whether Meena can use the customer's words to pick one of the two drinks, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Clear nimbu pani is uniform: its components cannot be seen even under a microscope. Masala nimbu pani is non-uniform: the mint leaves and cumin seeds can be seen with the naked eye. (b) The crust still tastes sweet and salty, so the sugar and salt kept their properties in the drink and did not react to form a new substance; they were got back by a physical process (letting the water go). (c) No. Both drinks are mixtures, the clear one uniform and the masala one non-uniform; in both the ingredients keep their own properties and do not react. Being uniform or non-uniform does not decide whether something new formed, so the customer's words fit both drinks and cannot pick one.
s: (a) clear drink uniform, masala drink non-uniform, with deciding observations
(b) sugar and salt kept their tastes and were recovered, so no new substance
(c) no: both are mixtures with unchanged ingredients; the type does not decide

questions.q: A canteen worker says that besan batter and sugar syrup must be the same type of mixture, because both look smooth to the naked eye. Differentiate between a uniform and a non-uniform mixture, and explain what further observation would be needed to place each of these two in its group.
questions.a: In a uniform mixture the components are evenly distributed and cannot be distinguished even with a microscope; in a non-uniform mixture the components are visible with the naked eye or a magnifying device. Looking smooth to the naked eye is not enough. Each must be examined with a magnifying glass and then a microscope: if separate components are seen, it is non-uniform; if nothing separate is seen even under a microscope, it is uniform.
s: correct difference based on whether components can be distinguished, even under a microscope
naked eye not enough; magnifier and microscope check decides each

questions.q:
Neel's notebook classifies four items.
(i) Sprout salad: uniform mixture, because all the pieces are mixed evenly.
(ii) Sugar dissolved in water: uniform mixture.
(iii) Lemonade stirred until clear: a pure substance, because it looks the same throughout.
(iv) Brass: a mixture of copper and zinc.
Find the two wrong entries and correct each, giving the reason.
questions.a: Entry (i) is wrong: a sprout salad is a non-uniform mixture, because its green gram, chickpeas, onion and tomato can be seen with the naked eye; even mixing does not make them invisible. Entry (iii) is wrong: lemonade is a mixture (of lemon juice, sugar and water), and a uniform one; looking the same throughout means its components cannot be told apart, not that only one substance is present. Entries (ii) and (iv) are correct.
s: identifies (i) and (iii) as the wrong entries
corrects (i): non-uniform, components visible
corrects (iii): uniform mixture, not a pure substance

questions.q:
A metal workshop has three unlabelled bars, X, Y and Z, each of which looks the same throughout even under a microscope. The owner knows that the three bars are the three alloys named in the chapter (stainless steel, brass and bronze), one bar each, and also this: X contains no copper; Y contains no tin; Z contains tin.
(a) Name the alloy that each bar is, and the metals in Y, explaining how you decided. (2)
(b) Explain why each bar is a mixture, and a uniform one, even though it is made of more than one metal. (2)
(c) The owner wants to tell Y from Z without the records. Explain why looking through a magnifying glass for separate metals cannot help him. (1)
questions.a: (a) X has no copper, and brass and bronze both contain copper, so X is stainless steel (iron, nickel, chromium and a little carbon). Z contains tin, so Z is bronze (copper and tin). Y has no tin, so it is not bronze; it must be brass, made of copper and zinc. (b) Each bar is made of two or more substances mixed together that each keep their properties and do not react chemically, so each is a mixture (an alloy). Because the metals are mixed so evenly that no single metal can be seen separately, even under a microscope, each is a uniform mixture. (c) In a uniform mixture the components cannot be distinguished at all, so neither brass nor bronze shows separate metals under a magnifying glass; he needs to know which metals each contains, not what it looks like.
s: (a) X stainless steel (no copper), Z bronze (tin), Y brass of copper and zinc by elimination
(b) components mixed without reacting, so a mixture; mixed so evenly none can be seen, so uniform
(c) no component of a uniform mixture can be seen, so the magnifier cannot separate brass from bronze

questions.q: Think of two everyday mixtures that are NOT in the chapter (not poha, sprout salad, sugar water, air, soup, lemonade or an alloy): one uniform and one non-uniform. For each, state the observation (with the naked eye, a magnifying glass or a microscope) that decides its type, and name one property that one of its components keeps in the mixture.
questions.a: Any correct pair, for example: Uniform - salt fully dissolved in water for gargling: nothing can be seen separately even under a microscope; the salt keeps its salty taste. Non-uniform - a mix of mustard seeds and cumin seeds for tadka: the two kinds of seed are seen with the naked eye; the mustard seeds keep their round shape and black colour.
s: a uniform example with the observation that it shows no separate components
a non-uniform example with the observation that its components are visible
a property kept by a component in the mixture

questions.q: A clear, colourless liquid is heated gently in a dish. The steam is cooled back into water, and a sweet white solid is left in the dish. The solid dissolves in water again to give the same clear liquid. What can be concluded about the original liquid?
questions.a: A mixture, as a physical process separated it
o: A mixture, as a physical process separated it
A pure substance that only changed its state
A pure compound broken down into its elements
A pure substance, because it looked clear

questions.q: True or false? 'When a chemist separates a mixture, her aim is different from a cook straining tea: the chemist is trying to obtain pure substances, not just the one part she happens to want.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. In everyday life a mixture is separated to obtain the component of interest, and the other components are discarded (the cook keeps the tea and throws away the leaves). In science, the purpose of separating a mixture is to obtain pure substances.
s: verdict: true
everyday separation keeps the wanted part; in science the aim is pure substances

questions.q:
A school canteen in Vijayawada buys 25 kg of turmeric powder a year and wants proof that nothing has been added to it. Three suppliers reply.
Supplier | Price per kg | Label on packet | Lab report sent
S1 | Rs 280 | 'Pure turmeric' | 'Only turmeric, nothing added. Note: turmeric itself contains many different substances.'
S2 | Rs 190 | 'Pure turmeric' | 'Turmeric with a cheap yellow powder added.'
S3 | Rs 250 | no claim | none sent
The canteen can get one sample tested by the same lab for Rs 600 a year. Assume S3's turmeric would pass the test.
(a) Which supplier is adulterating, and how does its price fit the reason the chapter gives for adulteration?
(b) Using S1's lab note, explain in which sense the word 'pure' on S1's packet is true and in which sense it is not.
(c) Which is the cheaper way for the canteen to get lab proof that nothing was added: buying from S1, or buying from S3 and paying for its own test? Show the yearly cost of each choice.
questions.a: (a) S2. Adulteration is adding a cheaper or poorer-quality substance to a product, usually to increase the quantity or reduce the cost; the added cheap powder lets S2 sell at only Rs 190 per kg. (b) It is true in the everyday sense: the turmeric is unadulterated. It is not pure in the scientific sense, because the lab note says turmeric itself contains many different substances, and a pure substance has no other substance present. (c) S1: 280 x 25 = Rs 7,000. S3 with a test: 250 x 25 + 600 = 6,250 + 600 = Rs 6,850. S3 with its own test costs Rs 150 less and still gives lab proof that nothing was added, so buying from S3 and having it tested is the cheaper way (S1's label 'pure' adds nothing that the test would not show).
s: (a) S2, cheap powder added to increase quantity or cut cost, hence the low price
(b) pure in the everyday sense; not a pure substance in science, using the lab note
(c) Rs 7,000 vs Rs 6,850; choose S3 with its own test

Statement 2: Ice, liquid water and water vapour obtained from the same water are made of the same particles.
Statement 3: If a powder is passed through a fine sieve and nothing is caught, the powder must be a pure substance.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only

questions.q:
A recipe card lists the components of a glass of sweet lemon water as 'lemon juice, sugar and water'. The lemon juice is itself made of many substances; the sugar and the water are each a single substance.
(a) Which items on the card would a scientist accept as components of the mixture? Give the reason.
(b) What would the scientist have to do with the lemon juice before she could list all the true components?
questions.a: (a) Only the sugar and the water. In science, all the components of a mixture must be pure substances; lemon juice is itself a mixture, so in common usage it is a component but not in the scientific sense. (b) She would have to separate the lemon juice further until she obtained the pure substances it contains; those pure substances, with the sugar and water, are the scientific components.
s: (a) sugar and water only, as scientific components must be pure substances
(b) separate the lemon juice into the pure substances it contains

questions.q: A gas jar is found to contain only oxygen molecules, each made of two oxygen atoms. Is the gas in the jar a pure substance?
questions.a: Yes, as its particles are all one type
o: Yes, as its particles are all one type
No, as each of its particles has two atoms
No, as a gas is always a mixture of gases
Yes, but only once it has been made liquid

questions.q: Tara takes ice made from pure water, melts it, boils the water into vapour, and then cools the vapour back into water. She says, 'All along I had the same pure substance; only its state changed.' Is she right? Support your verdict with what happens to the particles and with evidence from the changes.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. During melting, boiling and cooling the particles of water remain the same; only the state changes. The evidence is that the changes can be reversed: heating ice gives back water and cooling water vapour gives back water, the same substance she started with. No other kind of matter was separated or formed.
s: verdict: she is right
the particles of water stay the same in every state
evidence: water is got back on heating ice and on cooling the vapour

questions.q: From the list sugar, salt water, iron, air, oxygen gas and lemonade, pick out only the pure substances. Together, those pure substances contain ___ different elements.

Isha designs a 'purity check' for unknown samples.
Step 1: Look at the sample with a magnifying glass and then a microscope. If separate components are seen, call it a mixture.
Step 2: If nothing separate is seen, call it a pure substance.
(a) Apply Isha's check to a sprout salad and to sugar dissolved in water, and say for which sample it gives a wrong result. (2)
(b) Explain, using the chapter's definition of a pure substance, why Step 2 is faulty. (2)
(c) Rewrite Step 2 so that it matches the chapter's definition. (1)
questions.a: (a) Sprout salad: components are seen, so it is called a mixture, which is correct. Sugar water: nothing is seen even under a microscope, so Step 2 calls it pure, which is wrong; it is a uniform mixture. (b) In a uniform mixture the components cannot be distinguished even under a microscope, so seeing nothing does not prove that only one substance is present. The chapter defines a pure substance as one with no other substance present, made of the same type of particles, that cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any physical process; sugar water can be separated (evaporating the water leaves the sugar), so it is not pure. (c) If nothing separate is seen, try physical processes such as filtering and evaporating; call the sample pure only if no physical process separates it into other kinds of matter.
s: (a) salad correctly a mixture; sugar water wrongly called pure
(b) uniform mixtures show nothing under a microscope; pure means no physical process can separate it, and sugar water can be separated
(c) rewritten step: call it pure only if no physical process separates it

Reason (R): Sugar is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
Gold dust is stirred into sugar.
(a) Gold is an element and sugar is a compound, yet each is a pure substance on its own. State what makes each of them pure.
(b) Now explain why the stirred sample is not a pure substance, and name a physical process that would show it.
questions.a: (a) Each has no other substance present in it and consists of the same type of particles throughout. (b) The stirred sample has two kinds of particles, gold and sugar, each keeping its own properties. A physical process separates them: for example, dissolving the sugar in water and filtering out the gold. So it is a mixture, not a pure substance.
s: (a) no other substance present; the same type of particles throughout
(b) two kinds of particles; a physical process such as dissolving and filtering separates them

questions.q: A trader takes sugar, which is a pure substance, and mixes a cheaper white powder into it to sell more kilograms. Show that the adulterated sugar cannot be a pure substance in the scientific sense, even though the sugar he started with was pure.
questions.a: Adulteration means adding another, cheaper substance to the product, so the packet now holds at least two substances. A pure substance has no other substance present and consists of only one type of particle, so the adulterated sugar breaks the definition. Also, the sugar and the powder each keep their properties and could be separated by a physical process (for example, dissolving the sugar in water and filtering off the powder if it does not dissolve), which is impossible for a pure substance.
s: adulteration adds a second substance to the product
two types of particles breaks the definition of a pure substance
the components could be separated by a physical process, which a pure substance never allows

questions.q:
Match each sample with the physical process that would separate it into other kinds of matter, or with 'none' if no physical process can.
Column A:
1. Salt fully dissolved in water
2. Iron filings stirred into sand
3. Tea with tea leaves in it
4. A packet of sugar with nothing added
Column B:
a. Moving a magnet over it
b. None, as it is a pure substance
c. Letting the water evaporate
d. Straining or filtering

A teacher gives four sealed jars, J1 to J4, and says that one holds an element, one a compound, one a uniform mixture and one a non-uniform mixture. Her clues:
J1: a white solid; when heated strongly in a boiling tube it turns brown, then chars black, and water droplets form near the mouth of the tube.
J2: a clear liquid; nothing is seen separately even under a microscope; when a drop is evaporated gently, a white solid is left.
J3: cannot be broken down into simpler substances by any means.
J4: two kinds of grain can be seen with the naked eye.
(a) Which two jars hold pure substances? Give the clue that rules out each of the other two.
(b) Which pure substance is the element and which is the compound? Give the reason for each.
(c) Explain why J2 is a mixture although it looks like a single clear liquid even under a microscope.
(d) Work backwards: the teacher reveals that J2 was made by dissolving some of the J1 solid in water. What is the white solid left when J2 is evaporated, and is it a pure substance?
questions.a: (a) J1 and J3. J2 leaves a white solid when evaporated, so a physical process separates it; J4 shows two kinds of grain to the naked eye. Both are mixtures. (b) J3 is the element: it cannot be broken down into simpler substances. J1 is the compound: on heating it breaks down into carbon (the black char) and water, which is made of hydrogen and oxygen, so it contains more than one element. (c) In a uniform mixture the components are evenly spread and cannot be distinguished even under a microscope; J2 is shown to be a mixture because evaporation, a physical process, separates the white solid from the water. (d) It is the J1 substance got back unchanged; it is a pure substance (a compound), since it kept its properties in the mixture and only the water was removed.
s: (a) J1 and J3, with J2 ruled out by evaporation and J4 by visible grains
(b) J3 element (cannot be broken down); J1 compound (gives carbon and water)
(c) uniform mixtures look single even under a microscope; evaporation separates J2
(d) the solid is the J1 substance recovered, a pure substance

questions.q:
A lab tests 40 grains of a white powder one at a time, each in a large beaker of water stirred for a long time. 28 grains dissolve completely; the other 12 stay unchanged however much more water is added.
(a) What percentage of the grains behaved differently from the rest?
(b) What does this result tell you about whether the powder is a pure substance?
questions.a: (a) 12 / 40 x 100 = 30%. (b) It is not a pure substance. All the constituent particles of a pure substance behave identically, but here 30% of the grains behave differently even with plenty of water, so the powder contains at least two different substances and is a mixture.
s: (b) not pure: in a pure substance all particles behave alike, so two substances are present

questions.q: Pooja lists the components of a fruit salad as 'apple, banana and grapes'. Her teacher says this list is fine in everyday language but not in the scientific sense of 'component'. Why?
questions.a: Each fruit is itself made of many substances
o: Each fruit is itself made of many substances
A fruit salad is a uniform mixture of its fruits
The fruits react with each other once they are mixed
A mixture can have only two components

questions.q: Describe a real product that a shopkeeper and a scientist could both correctly call 'pure'. For your product, explain what the shopkeeper's word promises and what the scientist's word means, and say why both are true.
questions.a: Any correct example, such as a packet of sugar with nothing added. The shopkeeper's 'pure' promises that the product is unadulterated: no cheaper or poorer-quality substance has been added. The scientist's 'pure' means it has no other substance present and consists of the same type of particles (sugar is a compound, and a compound is a pure substance). Both are true because nothing else has been added and the product is a single substance.
s: a suitable product that is a single substance with nothing added
the shopkeeper's meaning: unadulterated
the scientist's meaning: only one type of particle, and why it holds

questions.q:
At home, Ritu strains her tea and throws the leaves away. In a lab, a chemist separates the same tea and keeps every part.
(a) Explain the difference between their aims.
(b) The chemist separates one part again and again. When can she stop and call that part finished?
questions.a: (a) Ritu wants only the component of interest (the liquid tea) and discards the rest; the chemist's aim, as in all scientific separation, is to obtain pure substances, so no part is simply thrown away. (b) When no physical process can separate that part into any other kind of matter, because then it consists of only one type of particle: it is a pure substance.
s: (a) everyday aim: the wanted part; scientific aim: pure substances
(b) stop when no physical process separates it further, i.e. it is pure

questions.q:
Compare oxygen gas, common salt and salt fully dissolved in water.
(a) For each, state whether it is made of one type of particle or more than one. (1)
(b) Which of the three can be separated into other kinds of matter by a physical process? Name the process and what it gives. (1)
(c) Which of the three is a compound, and why can its elements not be separated from it by evaporation or filtering? (2)
(d) Using only your answers to (a) and (b), decide which two of the three are most alike, and justify. (1)
questions.a: (a) Oxygen: one type of particle. Common salt: one type of particle (sodium chloride). Salt water: more than one (salt and water). (b) Only salt water: evaporating the water leaves the salt behind. (c) Common salt (sodium chloride) is the compound: it is made of sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio. (Oxygen is an element, and salt water is a mixture.) In a compound the elements are combined chemically, and the constituent elements cannot be separated by any physical method, so evaporation or filtering leaves the salt unchanged. (d) Oxygen and common salt: both are made of one type of particle and neither can be separated by a physical process, so both are pure substances, while salt water is a mixture.
s: (a) oxygen and salt one type of particle; salt water more than one
(b) only salt water, by evaporation, giving salt
(c) common salt is the compound; its sodium and chlorine are combined chemically, which physical methods cannot separate
(d) oxygen and salt, both pure substances

questions.q: A food inspector visits four shops. Which shop is doing what the chapter calls adulteration?
questions.a: Selling chilli powder bulked up with brick dust
o: Selling chilli powder bulked up with brick dust
Selling sweetened milk labelled 'with added sugar'
Selling brass vessels made by mixing copper and zinc
Selling sugar syrup made by dissolving sugar in water

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Water cannot be called an element.
Reason (R): Passing electric current through water breaks it down into two simpler substances, hydrogen and oxygen.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: In a demonstration of passing electricity through acidified water, two test tubes of gas are collected. A burning candle brought near tube P gives a pop sound; near tube Q the candle flame glows brighter. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: P held hydrogen and Q held oxygen
o: P held hydrogen and Q held oxygen
P held oxygen and Q held hydrogen
Both held water vapour from the water
Both held hydrogen, in different amounts

questions.q:
Group 3 in a Bengaluru school watched their teacher pass electric current from a 9 V battery through water with a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid. Their record:
Observation 1: bubbles formed at both terminals and gas collected in both test tubes.
Observation 2: tube A - a burning candle held near it gave a pop sound.
Observation 3: tube B - the candle flame glowed brighter.
Conclusion 1: Water is a mixture of hydrogen gas and oxygen gas, and the battery simply separated them, just as a filter separates sand from water.
Conclusion 2: The two gases collected are elements.
(a) Name the gas in each tube, giving the observation that identifies it.
(b) Find the error in Conclusion 1 and correct it.
(c) The group could not break the collected hydrogen down into anything simpler. Explain why this is expected, using Conclusion 2.
(d) Decide which sentence should end their report, and justify: 'Water is an element', 'Water is made of the elements hydrogen and oxygen', or 'Water contains hydrogen gas and oxygen gas mixed together'.
questions.a: (a) Tube A: hydrogen, since it gave a pop sound with the burning candle. Tube B: oxygen, since the candle flame glowed brighter. (b) Water is not a mixture of the two gases. Water is a pure substance; the electric current broke water down into two new substances, hydrogen and oxygen, which were not present as gases in it. Filtering is a physical process that only separates components already present. (c) Hydrogen is an element, and elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances. (d) 'Water is made of the elements hydrogen and oxygen'. Water is broken down by the current, so it is not an element; and the gases were formed from water, not mixed in it, so the third sentence is wrong.
s: (a) A hydrogen (pop), B oxygen (brighter flame)
(b) water is not a mixture of the gases; it was broken down into new substances, not filtered apart
(c) hydrogen is an element, which cannot be broken down further
(d) chooses 'made of the elements hydrogen and oxygen' and rules out the other two

questions.q: Ravi melts a lump of sulfur in a test tube and lets it cool; it becomes solid sulfur again. He says, 'This proves sulfur is an element.' What is the best response?
questions.a: Not enough; a change of state cannot show it
o: Not enough; a change of state cannot show it
Yes; whatever melts back unchanged is an element
No; sulfur must be a compound, since it melts
Yes; every yellow solid is an element

questions.q: True or false? 'Every element exists as single, separate atoms.' Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The atoms of most elements cannot exist independently. Two or more atoms combine to form a stable particle of the element called a molecule; for example, two atoms of hydrogen combine to form one molecule of hydrogen, and two atoms of oxygen form one molecule of oxygen.
s: verdict: false
atoms of most elements join into molecules, e.g. two hydrogen atoms form one hydrogen molecule

questions.q: When some water is broken down by electric current, 1,200 atoms of hydrogen are set free, and they join in the way the chapter describes for hydrogen gas. The number of hydrogen molecules formed is ___.

(a) Under the chapter's meaning of an element, what is true of every atom in a bar of pure gold?
(b) A bangle sold as 'gold' is found to contain some copper as well. Explain whether the bangle is the element gold.
questions.a: (a) Every atom is a gold atom: an element is made of identical atoms, and they are different from the atoms of any other element. (b) No. The bangle contains copper atoms as well as gold atoms, so its atoms are not all identical; it is a mixture of two elements (gold and copper), not the element gold.
s: (a) all atoms identical gold atoms, different from other elements' atoms
(b) two kinds of atoms, so a mixture, not the element

questions.q: Zoya says, 'Oxygen is an element because it is a gas, and water is not an element because it is a liquid.' Judge her statement: what is right in it and what is wrong?
questions.a: Partly right. Her conclusions are correct: oxygen is an element and water is not. Her reasons are wrong: the state (gas or liquid) does not decide whether a substance is an element. Oxygen is an element because it is made of identical atoms and cannot be broken down into simpler substances; water is not an element because electric current breaks it down into hydrogen and oxygen. (Hydrogen is also a gas, while gold and silver are solid elements.)
s: verdict: partly right; the conclusions are correct
the reasons are wrong: state does not decide
the correct reasons: identical atoms, cannot be broken down; water is broken down by current

questions.q:
Compare two things done to water: (i) boiling water in a kettle, and (ii) passing electric current through water with a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid.
(a) What is the gas formed in each case? (1)
(b) What happens when each gas is cooled? (1)
(c) Explain what each case shows about the particles of water. (2)
(d) Which case gives elements, and how is this confirmed? (1)
questions.a: (a) Boiling gives water vapour; electric current gives two gases, hydrogen and oxygen. (b) Water vapour condenses back into water; hydrogen and oxygen do not turn back into water on cooling. (c) In boiling the particles of water remain the same; only the state changes, and water is got back. With electric current the water itself is broken down into two different substances, so its particles do not stay as water. (d) Case (ii): the gas that gives a pop sound with a burning candle is hydrogen and the gas that makes the flame glow brighter is oxygen; both are elements.
s: (a) vapour in (i); hydrogen and oxygen in (ii)
(b) vapour condenses to water; the two gases do not
(c) (i) particles unchanged, only state changes; (ii) water broken down into new substances
(d) (ii), confirmed by the pop test and the brighter-flame test

questions.q: A sample of pure silver is heated strongly, melted, cooled and ground to powder, and other methods are tried too, but no method ever gives anything simpler than silver. What does this show?
questions.a: Silver is an element with nothing simpler in it
o: Silver is an element with nothing simpler in it
Silver is a compound held together too tightly
Silver is a uniform mixture of identical metals
Silver can only be split by a 9 V battery

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: The atoms of gold are different from the atoms of silver.
Statement 2: The hydrogen and the oxygen obtained by passing electric current through water are both elements.
Statement 3: Carbon cannot be broken down into simpler substances.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: A student's notebook says: 'In my model of the hydrogen gas collected, there are 15 hydrogen atoms, all paired up into hydrogen molecules.' Show that this record cannot be right, and correct the number of atoms or molecules so that it could be.
questions.a: A molecule of hydrogen is formed when two atoms of hydrogen combine. If every atom is paired into molecules, the number of atoms must be 2 x (number of molecules), an even number. 15 is odd: 7 molecules use 14 atoms and one atom is left unpaired, so 'all paired up' is impossible. A possible correction: 14 atoms forming 7 molecules (or 16 atoms forming 8 molecules).
s: each hydrogen molecule has two atoms
so the atom count must be even; 15 leaves one atom unpaired
a correct pair, e.g. 14 atoms and 7 molecules

questions.q:
During the electricity-through-water demonstration, the teacher lifts the 9 V battery out of the beaker for a minute: the bubbles stop, and start again when she puts it back. She then places the same battery in an empty, dry beaker: no gas forms at all.
(a) What do these two observations together show about where the gases come from?
(b) Do these observations alone prove that the gases are hydrogen and oxygen? State what further result would.
questions.a: (a) Gas forms only when the current passes through the water: the battery alone gives no gas and the water alone gives no gas. So the gases come from the water, broken down by the electric current (Water gives Hydrogen + Oxygen). (b) No; they only show that the water is breaking down. A burning candle must be brought near each tube: a pop sound shows hydrogen, and the flame glowing brighter shows oxygen.
s: (a) the gases come from water broken down by the current; neither alone gives gas
(b) no; the pop test and the brighter-flame test are needed

questions.q: Gas jar P holds only hydrogen molecules and gas jar Q holds only oxygen molecules. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Each jar holds one element, and their atoms differ
o: Each jar holds one element, and their atoms differ
Both jars hold the same element, as both are gases
Jar Q holds a compound, as each molecule has two atoms
Both jars hold compounds made of two atoms each

questions.q:
Match each sample with what the observation shows it to be.
Column A:
1. Water: electric current breaks it into two gases
2. Sugar: heating leaves carbon and gives water droplets
3. Silver: no method gives anything simpler
4. A sealed jar into which hydrogen and oxygen were let in, without any reaction
Column B:
a. An element
b. A substance broken down by heating, so not an element
c. A mixture of two elements
d. A substance broken down by electricity, so not an element

Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas are let into one sealed jar, where they do not react.
(a) How many elements are in the jar, and is its content an element, a compound or a mixture?
(b) Water also contains only hydrogen and oxygen. State one way the jar's content differs from water.
questions.a: (a) Two elements, hydrogen and oxygen; the content is a mixture, since the two are only mixed and each keeps its own properties. (b) Any one: in water hydrogen and oxygen are combined chemically in a fixed 2:1 ratio of atoms and cannot be separated by physical methods; water has properties different from both (it puts out fire, while hydrogen is a fuel and oxygen supports burning). In the jar, each gas keeps its own properties.
s: (a) two elements; a mixture
(b) one valid difference: chemically combined in a fixed ratio, or new properties, in water

questions.q:
A teacher in Kolkata uses bead models to explain the electricity-through-water activity. Each white bead is a hydrogen atom and each red bead an oxygen atom. In water the ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms is 2:1. After the model 'reaction', tray X holds 40 white pairs (each pair is one molecule of the gas that pops with a flame) and tray Y holds 20 red pairs (each one molecule of the gas that makes a flame glow brighter). The numbers are illustrative.
(a) Name the gas shown in each tray.
(b) How many atoms of each element are in the trays altogether?
(c) Work backwards: how many water molecules must have been broken down to give these trays? Show that both trays agree.
(d) Sonal says tray Y should hold as many molecules as tray X, because 'each water molecule gives one hydrogen and one oxygen'. Judge her reasoning.
questions.a: (a) Tray X: hydrogen. Tray Y: oxygen. (b) 40 x 2 = 80 hydrogen atoms; 20 x 2 = 40 oxygen atoms. (c) Each water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. 80 hydrogen atoms / 2 = 40 water molecules; 40 oxygen atoms / 1 = 40 water molecules. Both give 40. (d) She is wrong. Each water molecule gives 2 hydrogen atoms (one whole hydrogen molecule) but only 1 oxygen atom, which is half an oxygen molecule, since an oxygen molecule needs two atoms. So 40 water molecules give 40 hydrogen molecules but only 20 oxygen molecules.
s: (a) X hydrogen, Y oxygen
(b) 80 hydrogen atoms and 40 oxygen atoms
(c) 40 water molecules from both trays
(d) wrong: one water gives one hydrogen molecule but half an oxygen molecule

questions.q: A student's list of elements reads 'gold, sulfur, sugar, carbon'. Which entry does not belong, and why?
questions.a: Sugar, as heating breaks it into carbon and water
o: Sugar, as heating breaks it into carbon and water
Carbon, as it is a black solid and not a metal
Sulfur, as it melts easily when it is heated
Gold, as it is usually found mixed with rock in nature

questions.q: Arjun watches the electricity-through-water demonstration and says, 'The battery just heats the water, so the bubbles are only steam.' Is he right? Give two reasons from the activity.
questions.a: No. (1) If the gases were water vapour (steam), they would condense back to form water in the test tubes, but they stay as gases. (2) The two gases behave differently from water vapour and from each other: one makes a burning candle give a pop sound (hydrogen) and the other makes the flame glow brighter (oxygen). So water has been broken down into two new substances, not just turned into vapour.
s: verdict: no
water vapour would condense back into water; these gases do not
the gases pass the hydrogen and oxygen tests, so they are new substances

questions.q:
A teacher describes five substances, P to T.
P: when heated strongly it chars and leaves carbon, and water droplets form.
Q: electric current breaks it down into two gases.
R: no method breaks it down into anything simpler.
S: made only of identical atoms, which join in pairs to form molecules.
T: made of particles that each contain atoms of two different kinds.
(a) Classify each of P, Q, R, S and T as 'element' or 'not an element', with a one-line reason for each. (3)
(b) The chapter's examples of elements include gold, silver, sulfur, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Name the elements that the clues show can be obtained from P and Q if Q is water, and explain how this supports the idea that elements are the building blocks of all matter. (2)
questions.a: (a) P: not an element; it breaks down into carbon and water. Q: not an element; it breaks down into two gases. R: element; it cannot be broken down into simpler substances. S: element; it is made of identical atoms (joined as molecules, like hydrogen and oxygen). T: not an element; its particles contain two kinds of atoms, while an element has identical atoms. (b) From P: carbon, plus hydrogen and oxygen from the water formed. From Q (water): hydrogen and oxygen. Two quite different substances turn out to be built from the same few elements, which cannot themselves be broken down, so elements are the building blocks from which other matter is made.
s: (a) P, Q, T not elements; R, S elements, each with a correct reason
(b) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen named, and linked to elements as building blocks

questions.q:
(a) The chapter says that elements and compounds are the building blocks of matter. Hydrogen, oxygen and water all appear in the electricity-through-water activity. Which of these three are building blocks in this sense?
(b) The chapter also calls elements the simplest substances. Which of the three are the simplest, and how does the activity show it?
questions.a: (a) All three: hydrogen and oxygen are elements and water is a compound, and the chapter calls both elements and compounds building blocks of matter. (b) Hydrogen and oxygen. The activity breaks water down into hydrogen and oxygen, so water is made of simpler substances; hydrogen and oxygen are elements, which cannot be broken down into anything simpler.
s: (a) all three: two elements and a compound
(b) hydrogen and oxygen; water breaks into them, and elements cannot be broken down

questions.q:
(a) Why is water called a compound and not a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen?
(b) Say whether freezing water into ice and melting it again could separate the hydrogen from the oxygen, and why.
questions.a: (a) In water the particles of hydrogen and oxygen are so tightly attached, combined chemically in a fixed ratio (2:1 by atoms), that they cannot be separated by physical methods; water is an entirely new substance. (b) No. Freezing and melting are physical changes in which the particles of water stay the same; physical methods cannot separate the elements of a compound.
s: (a) hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio, not separable physically
(b) no: freezing and melting are physical and leave water particles unchanged

questions.q: Two watch glasses hold powders made from iron and sulfur. Powder X shows black and yellow specks; powder Y is a uniform black mass. A magnet moved over each pulls black specks out of X only. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: X is a mixture; Y is the compound iron sulfide
o: X is a mixture; Y is the compound iron sulfide
X is the compound iron sulfide; Y is a mixture
Both are mixtures, but Y has been ground finer
Both are compounds of iron and sulfur

questions.q: A sample of pure water contains 4,800 hydrogen atoms. The number of oxygen atoms in the sample is ___.

A group in Patna heated a teaspoon of sugar gently in a dry boiling tube under their teacher's supervision and wrote this record.
Observation 1: the sugar turned brown, then blackish.
Observation 2: small droplets of water formed inside the tube near its open end.
Observation 3: a black solid was left; it was scooped onto a watch glass.
Conclusion (i): The droplets are water vapour from the room's air that condensed at the mouth of the tube.
Conclusion (ii): The black solid is carbon (charcoal).
Conclusion (iii): Sugar is a mixture of carbon and water.
(a) Find the error in Conclusion (i) and correct it.
(b) Explain why Conclusion (iii) is wrong, even though heating gave carbon and water.
(c) Name all the elements sugar contains, and explain how the group can know about the two that they never saw directly.
(d) The group now heats some common salt gently in the same way and sees no change. A member says, 'So salt must be an element.' Decide whether this result supports her, and justify.
questions.a: (a) The tube was being heated, so the water did not come from the air; it came from the sugar itself as it broke down on heating. (b) Sugar is not a mixture: it shows no carbon particles or water before heating, and carbon and water are new substances formed only when sugar decomposes. The elements in sugar are combined chemically to form something entirely new, so sugar is a compound. (c) Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen and oxygen were not seen as gases, but the water formed is made of hydrogen and oxygen, so they must have come from the sugar. (d) No. Failing to break a substance down by one gentle heating does not prove it cannot be broken down at all. Common salt is in fact sodium chloride, a compound of sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio.
s: (a) the water came from the sugar, since the tube was hot, not from the air
(b) carbon and water are new substances formed on decomposition; sugar is a compound
(c) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen; hydrogen and oxygen known from the water formed
(d) no: one failed method does not prove an element; salt is sodium chloride, a compound

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The iron in iron sulfide can be pulled out with a magnet.
Reason (R): In a mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder, the iron filings are attracted by a magnet.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: True or false? 'Common salt can be separated from water by evaporation, but evaporation cannot separate common salt into sodium and chlorine.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Salt water is a mixture, so its components can be separated by a physical process such as evaporation. Common salt (sodium chloride) is a compound: its sodium and chlorine are combined chemically in a 1:1 ratio, and the constituent elements of a compound cannot be separated by any physical method.
s: verdict: true
salt water is a mixture separable physically; sodium chloride is a compound whose elements cannot be separated physically

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: The ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms is the same in every sample of pure water.
Statement 2: In a mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder, both components react with dilute hydrochloric acid.
Statement 3: Since salt can be got back from salt water by evaporation, sodium and chlorine can also be separated from each other by evaporation.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
(a) Iron filings mixed with sulfur powder (Sample A) are put in dilute hydrochloric acid. Which component reacts, and what gas is given off?
(b) Explain what the yellow solid left at the bottom of the test tube shows about the components of a mixture.
questions.a: (a) The iron reacts, forming iron chloride and hydrogen gas (colourless, no smell, burns with a pop). (b) The yellow solid is sulfur, which does not react with hydrochloric acid. It is left unchanged because in a mixture each component keeps its own properties: the iron behaves as iron and the sulfur as sulfur.
s: (a) iron reacts, giving hydrogen gas
(b) the sulfur is left unreacted, showing each component keeps its own properties

questions.q: Kiran says, 'Water is a compound simply because it is made of two elements.' Judge whether her reason is enough.
questions.a: Partly right. Water is a compound and it is made of two elements, hydrogen and oxygen. But being made of two elements is not enough: a mixture of hydrogen gas and oxygen gas, or the iron filings and sulfur powder of Sample A, also contains two elements. Water is a compound because its elements are combined chemically in a fixed ratio (2:1 by atoms), so tightly that physical methods cannot separate them, and it has properties different from both.
s: verdict: partly right; water is a compound of two elements
two elements alone also fit a mixture, e.g. Sample A
the missing idea: chemical combination in a fixed ratio, not separable physically, new properties

questions.q:
In a bead model, a teacher has 900 white beads (hydrogen atoms) and 600 red beads (oxygen atoms). She builds as many water molecules as she can, each from 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. The numbers are illustrative.
(a) What is the largest number of water molecules she can build? (1)
(b) Which beads are left over, and how many? (1)
(c) If the left-over beads are joined in the way the chapter describes for that element's gas, how many molecules do they make? (1)
(d) A student says, 'Use all 1,500 beads to make water; just put more oxygen into each molecule.' Explain, using the chapter, why the finished model must be described as water plus oxygen and not as one bigger lot of water. (2)
questions.a: (a) 900 / 2 = 450 molecules (enough oxygen, since 450 needs only 450 of the 600 red beads). (b) 600 - 450 = 150 oxygen beads; no hydrogen is left. (c) Oxygen atoms join in pairs: 150 / 2 = 75 oxygen molecules. (d) Water is a compound in which hydrogen and oxygen are combined in a fixed ratio of 2:1 by atoms; a particle with more oxygen would not be water. So only 450 water molecules can form, and the 75 oxygen molecules stay as a separate substance; together they make a mixture of water and oxygen.
s: (a) 450 water molecules
(b) 150 oxygen beads left
(c) 75 oxygen molecules
(d) fixed 2:1 ratio means extra oxygen cannot be part of water; the result is water mixed with oxygen

questions.q: A student heats sugar strongly in a boiling tube. It leaves a black residue, and water droplets form near the mouth of the tube. Together, these observations show that sugar
questions.a: is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
o: is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
is a mixture of carbon and water
is an element that changes colour on heating
is a compound of carbon and water only

questions.q:
(a) In a bead model of pure common salt there are 250 beads standing for sodium particles. How many chlorine beads must there be?
(b) Using the fixed-ratio idea, explain why a model with 250 sodium beads and 300 chlorine beads cannot stand for pure sodium chloride alone.
questions.a: (a) 250, because sodium chloride has sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio. (b) A compound always has its elements in a fixed ratio. 250 sodium can combine with only 250 chlorine, so 50 chlorine beads are left over that are not part of sodium chloride; the model shows sodium chloride with extra chlorine, not the pure compound.
s: (a) 250 chlorine beads (1:1)
(b) only 250 chlorine can combine; 50 left over, so not pure sodium chloride

questions.q: After the iron and sulfur activity, Riya says, 'Iron sulfide is black like iron filings, but it is not iron with sulfur stuck to it. It is a new substance, because the magnet ignores it and the acid gives a different gas.' Do you agree? Support your verdict.
questions.a: Yes, I agree. Looking black like iron does not make it iron. Iron sulfide is not attracted by a magnet, while iron filings are; with dilute hydrochloric acid it gives hydrogen sulfide (rotten-egg odour) instead of the odourless hydrogen that iron gives. Its colour and texture are the same throughout, and iron and sulfur can no longer be separated, so it is a compound with completely different properties.
s: verdict: agree
magnet test: iron sulfide is not attracted, unlike iron
acid test: hydrogen sulfide instead of hydrogen; iron and sulfur cannot be separated

questions.q:
Match each test with its result.
Column A:
1. Iron and sulfur mixture (unheated) + dilute hydrochloric acid
2. Iron sulfide + dilute hydrochloric acid
3. The sulfur in the unheated mixture + dilute hydrochloric acid
4. Sugar heated strongly in a boiling tube
Column B:
a. A colourless gas with a rotten-egg odour is given off
b. Stays as a yellow solid at the bottom
c. A colourless, odourless gas that burns with a pop is given off
d. Leaves black carbon and gives water droplets
Hydrogen is a fuel and oxygen supports combustion, yet water made from them is used to put out fires. Which idea from the chapter explains this?
questions.a: A compound has properties unlike its elements
o: A compound has properties unlike its elements
Water holds hydrogen and oxygen as a mixture
Water contains too little hydrogen to burn
The hydrogen atoms are destroyed when water forms

questions.q: A student grinds the black mass formed by heating iron filings with sulfur, and looks at the powder through a magnifying glass. What will she see?
questions.a: One kind of black powder all through
o: One kind of black powder all through
Black iron specks among yellow sulfur specks
Only yellow specks, as the iron has gone
Shiny iron specks that a magnet can lift

questions.q:
Four groups in a Ranchi school each tried to make iron sulfide by heating iron filings with sulfur powder. Their teacher tested the products.
Group | Appearance | Magnet test | Gas with dilute hydrochloric acid
W | black and yellow specks | black specks pulled out | colourless, no smell, pops with a flame; yellow solid left
X | uniform black mass | not attracted | colourless, rotten-egg smell
Y | mostly black, a few yellow specks | a few black specks pulled out | faint rotten-egg smell; also pops with a flame
Z | yellow only | not attracted | no gas
(a) Which group made iron sulfide completely? Give two results that show it.
(b) Which group's sample seems never to have been heated, and which seems to contain no iron at all?
(c) Explain what Y's results show about what happened when it was heated.
(d) Using the magnet and gas results, rank W, X and Y from the most to the least iron that has combined with sulfur, and justify the place of each.
questions.a: (a) X: it is not attracted by a magnet, and with acid it gives a gas with a rotten-egg smell (hydrogen sulfide); it is also uniform black. (b) W behaves like the unheated mixture (both colours seen, iron pulled out, hydrogen given off, sulfur left). Z contains no iron: no magnetic specks and no gas with acid, only yellow sulfur. (c) Some iron and sulfur combined to form iron sulfide (rotten-egg smell), but some iron and sulfur were left uncombined: the yellow specks are sulfur, the magnetic specks are iron, and the iron gives hydrogen that pops. So Y is a mixture of iron sulfide with leftover iron and sulfur. (d) X, then Y, then W. In X no iron is pulled out by the magnet and no hydrogen is given off, so all the iron has combined into iron sulfide. Y gives some hydrogen sulfide but also some iron that a magnet lifts and that gives hydrogen, so only part of the iron combined. W behaves like the unheated mixture: iron is pulled out and only hydrogen forms, so no iron combined.
s: (a) X, with two correct results (not magnetic, rotten-egg gas, uniform)
(b) W looks unheated; Z has no iron
(c) Y partly reacted: iron sulfide plus leftover iron and sulfur
(d) X > Y > W, each placed using magnet and gas evidence

questions.q:
(a) Write the word equations for what happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to the iron in the unheated iron-sulfur mixture, and to iron sulfide.
(b) One product is the same in both. Name it, and say what the difference between the other products shows about where the sulfur is in each sample.
questions.a: (a) Iron + Dilute hydrochloric acid gives Iron chloride + Hydrogen. Iron sulfide + Dilute hydrochloric acid gives Iron chloride + Hydrogen sulfide. (b) Iron chloride appears in both. In the mixture the sulfur does not react and stays as a yellow solid, so only hydrogen forms; in iron sulfide the sulfur is combined with the iron, so a gas containing it, hydrogen sulfide (rotten-egg odour), forms.
s: (a) both word equations correct
(b) iron chloride common; hydrogen sulfide shows sulfur combined in the compound, while in the mixture sulfur stays unreacted

questions.q:
A health poster says: 'Common salt contains chlorine, which is a hazardous gas, so eating salt must be hazardous to health.'
(a) Which part of the poster's information is correct?
(b) Explain the error in its reasoning.
questions.a: (a) It is correct that common salt (sodium chloride) contains chlorine, combined with sodium in a 1:1 ratio, and that chlorine on its own is a hazardous gas. (b) When elements combine to form a compound, the compound is an entirely new substance with properties different from those of its elements. Sodium chloride does not have chlorine's hazardous property; the chapter calls it harmless and essential for our lives.
s: (a) salt does contain chlorine (with sodium, 1:1), and chlorine alone is hazardous
(b) a compound's properties differ from its elements', so salt is harmless

questions.q: Using a compound from this chapter other than water, write a short situation for a Class 6 science corner that shows the idea 'the properties of a compound are different from those of the elements forming it'. Name the elements, the compound, and at least two properties that change.
questions.a: Any correct situation, for example: In a demonstration, black, magnetic iron filings and yellow sulfur powder are heated together to give a uniform black mass, iron sulfide. A magnet no longer attracts it, and with dilute hydrochloric acid it gives hydrogen sulfide, a gas with a rotten-egg smell, instead of the odourless hydrogen the iron gave. (Or: soft metal sodium and hazardous gas chlorine form harmless common salt that we eat.)
s: names the elements and the compound correctly
first property that is different in the compound
second property that is different in the compound

questions.q:
Compare and analyse how the parts of three samples could be obtained: (i) salt dissolved in water, (ii) iron filings mixed with sulfur powder, (iii) pure water.
(a) State a physical method that separates the parts of (i), and what it gives. (1)
(b) State a physical method that separates the parts of (ii), and what it shows about the iron. (1)
(c) Explain why no physical method can give hydrogen and oxygen from (iii), and state how the chapter does break water down. (2)
(d) Using (a)-(c), state what the difference tells you about mixtures and compounds. (1)
questions.a: (a) Evaporation: the water goes off and the salt is left. (b) Moving a magnet over it pulls out the iron filings; the iron keeps its magnetic property in the mixture. (c) In water the particles of hydrogen and oxygen are so tightly attached, combined chemically in a fixed ratio, that physical methods cannot separate them. The chapter breaks water down by passing electric current through it (with a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid), giving hydrogen and oxygen. (d) The components of a mixture keep their properties and can be separated by physical methods; the elements of a compound are combined chemically and cannot be separated physically.
s: (a) evaporation leaves the salt
(b) a magnet removes the iron, which kept its properties
(c) chemically combined elements resist physical methods; electric current breaks water down
(d) mixtures separable physically, compounds not

questions.q: A lab reports that the metal of a new bicycle frame is made of only one kind of atom, all identical. Which description fits the frame's metal?
questions.a: An element used directly, like aluminium
o: An element used directly, like aluminium
An alloy designed by engineers, like steel
A compound made by chemists, like a medicine
A building mixture, like concrete

questions.q:
A town council near Puri must build a bus-stop shelter frame close to the sea. The shelter must be strong, and the council wants the lowest cost for each year the frame lasts. It has Rs 45,000 available now. An engineer gives these illustrative figures for sea air:
Material | Cost of frame | Expected life
Pure iron | Rs 40,000 | 5 years
Stainless steel | Rs 70,000 | 25 years
Wood | Rs 30,000 | 3 years
(a) Classify each material as an element, a compound or a mixture.
(b) Work out the cost per year of life for each material.
(c) Which fact from the chapter fits the stainless steel figures, and what kind of work by engineers does it show?
(d) Decide which frame the council should buy now, within its Rs 45,000, and state what it gives up by not buying the best option.
questions.a: (a) Pure iron: element. Stainless steel: mixture (an alloy). Wood: mixture. (b) Iron: 40,000 / 5 = Rs 8,000 a year. Stainless steel: 70,000 / 25 = Rs 2,800 a year. Wood: 30,000 / 3 = Rs 10,000 a year. (c) The chapter says stainless steel is stronger and more durable than pure iron; engineers and material scientists use their understanding of mixtures to design materials with unique properties. (d) Stainless steel is cheapest per year but costs Rs 70,000, more than the Rs 45,000 available. Of the two it can afford, iron (Rs 8,000 a year) beats wood (Rs 10,000 a year), so it should buy the iron frame. It gives up the lower yearly cost (Rs 2,800) and the longer life of the stainless steel frame.
s: (a) iron element; stainless steel and wood mixtures
(b) Rs 8,000, Rs 2,800 and Rs 10,000 a year
(c) stainless steel is stronger and more durable than pure iron; a designed mixture
(d) iron within budget, beating wood; gives up stainless steel's lower yearly cost and longer life

questions.q: A school gate area has a wooden door, a steel gate, an aluminium ladder and a concrete wall. The number of these four items made of materials that the chapter calls mixtures is ___.
True or false? 'Fertilisers and medicines made by chemists are just mixtures of elements stirred together.' Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says chemists study how elements combine to create compounds, and this knowledge enables them to invent medicines and vaccines and to create fertilisers. Combining elements into compounds forms entirely new substances with new properties; stirring elements together would only make a mixture in which each element keeps its own properties.
s: verdict: false
chemists combine elements into new compounds, which is different from stirring them into a mixture

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: Wood used for furniture is an element, because it comes from a single tree.
Statement 2: The air we breathe is a mixture of gases such as oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide.
Statement 3: Water, which is essential for life, is a compound made of hydrogen and oxygen.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
(a) Air and water are both essential for life. Which of them is a mixture and which is a compound?
(b) Explain why water vapour can be taken out of air simply by cooling it on a cold surface, while hydrogen cannot be taken out of water by any such physical method.
questions.a: (a) Air is a mixture; water is a compound. (b) Water vapour is one component of air, the mixture, and it keeps its own properties, so it turns into droplets on a cool surface and leaves the air. In water, hydrogen and oxygen are combined chemically in a fixed ratio, and the elements of a compound cannot be separated by physical methods.
s: (a) air mixture, water compound
(b) a mixture's component can be removed physically; a compound's elements cannot

questions.q: Rohini says, 'Engineers should always use pure elements, because mixtures are impure, and impure things are weaker.' Do you agree? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. (1) The chapter's example goes the other way: stainless steel, a mixture, is stronger and more durable than pure iron, and engineers developed it for that reason. (2) In science 'impure' only means that more than one substance is present; it does not mean weak or poor. Engineers and material scientists design mixtures, such as alloys, wood, steel and concrete, to get unique properties.
s: verdict: disagree
stainless steel, a mixture, is stronger and more durable than pure iron
'impure' means more than one substance, not weaker; mixtures are designed for useful properties

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Iron and aluminium are used to construct bridges, buildings and vehicles.
Reason (R): Iron and aluminium are compounds made by chemists.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

Assertion (A): Wood, steel and concrete, used as building materials, are all mixtures.
Reason (R): Engineers and material scientists rely on their understanding of compounds and mixtures to design materials with unique properties.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
'Understanding elements, compounds and mixtures is the key to innovation.' A science exhibition in Nashik has four stalls:
Stall 1: a new fertiliser that raised a village's wheat yield.
Stall 2: a vaccine developed in a laboratory.
Stall 3: a concrete check dam built across a stream.
Stall 4: a bicycle frame of aluminium.
(a) For each stall, say whose knowledge it mainly shows: chemists combining elements into compounds, engineers designing compounds and mixtures, or an element used directly. (2)
(b) Which stall uses a material that the chapter says is a mixture? (1)
(c) Choose two stalls and use them to justify the statement in quotation marks. (2)
questions.a: (a) Stall 1: chemists' knowledge of how elements combine into compounds, used to create fertilisers. Stall 2: the same chemists' knowledge, used to invent vaccines and medicines. Stall 3: engineers' knowledge of mixtures (concrete). Stall 4: an element (aluminium) used directly. (b) Stall 3: concrete is a mixture. (c) Any two, for example: Stall 1 shows that knowing how elements combine into compounds led to fertilisers that increase crop production and help feed a growing population; Stall 2 shows the same knowledge led to life-saving vaccines. Both are new things that exist only because scientists understood how elements form compounds, so this understanding is the key to innovation.
s: (a) stalls 1 and 2 chemists; stall 3 engineers' mixture; stall 4 element used directly
(b) stall 3, concrete
(c) two stalls linked to new products made possible by this understanding

questions.q: Differentiate between using iron and using steel for the beams of a building, by stating what kind of matter each is and what that means for how the material got its properties.
questions.a: Iron is an element: it is used directly for the properties it has as a single substance. Steel is a mixture: its properties come from the substances that are mixed in it, so they can be chosen by deciding what to mix, which is how engineers and material scientists design materials with unique properties.
s: iron an element used for its own properties
steel a mixture whose properties come from what is mixed in it

questions.q: A new pipe material is made by mixing two substances; each keeps its own properties, but together they bend far less than either does alone. Which description fits?
questions.a: A mixture designed for a useful property
o: A mixture designed for a useful property
A compound made by chemists from elements
An element used directly for its strength
A pure substance with one kind of particle

questions.q: Vivek says, 'Everything used to build a house is a mixture.' Judge his claim, using the materials the chapter names.
questions.a: Partly right. Many building materials are mixtures: the chapter names wood, steel and concrete as building materials that are all mixtures. But elements are also used directly: iron and aluminium, which are elements, are used to construct buildings, bridges and vehicles. So 'everything' is too strong.
s: verdict: partly right
wood, steel and concrete are mixtures
iron and aluminium, elements, are also used in buildings

questions.q:
Match each thing with the description that fits it.

3. Concrete in a school wall
4. Water in a drinking bottle
Column B:
a. A compound essential for life
b. A mixture used as a building material
