A cycle shop's poster says: 'Frame: aluminium, an element. Chain: steel, an element.'
(a) Which label is wrong? Correct it.
(b) Explain what the corrected label tells you about where the chain's properties come from.
questions.a: (a) The chain label is wrong: steel is a mixture, not an element (the frame label is correct; aluminium is an element). (b) As a mixture, steel's properties come from the substances mixed in it, so a material with the properties needed can be designed by choosing what to mix, as engineers and material scientists do.
s: (a) chain label wrong: steel is a mixture
(b) a mixture's properties come from what is mixed, so they can be designed

questions.q: Write a short 'morning routine' of about four sentences in which you use at least one element, one compound and one mixture named in this chapter. After each, write in brackets whether it is an element, a compound or a mixture.
questions.a: Any correct routine, for example: I wake up and breathe in fresh air (mixture). I drink a glass of water (compound). I stir a spoon of sugar into my milk (sugar: compound). I ride to school on a bicycle with an aluminium frame (element) and lock it to a steel railing (mixture).
s: an element from the chapter used correctly and labelled
a compound from the chapter used correctly and labelled
a mixture from the chapter used correctly and labelled

questions.q:
For an exhibition, Aarav made a chart titled 'What things are, and how we use them'.
Row 1: Air - a compound - breathed by living beings.
Row 2: Water - a compound of hydrogen and oxygen - essential for life.
Row 3: Aluminium - a mixture - used to make vehicles.
Row 4: Concrete - an element - used as a building material.
Row 5: Wood - a mixture - used as a building material.
(a) Which rows are correct as they stand?
(b) Correct each of the other rows, giving the right kind of matter.
(c) Aarav wants to add the caption 'Engineers design mixtures with unique properties' beside one row. Decide whether Row 4 or Row 5 is the better place for it, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Rows 2 and 5. (b) Row 1: air is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide. Row 3: aluminium is an element. Row 4: concrete is a mixture. (c) Row 4. Concrete and wood are both mixtures used for building, but concrete is made by people by deciding what to mix, so its properties are designed; wood grows as it is, so no engineer designed its mixture. The caption fits the material whose mixture people design.
s: (a) rows 2 and 5
(b) air a mixture, aluminium an element, concrete a mixture
(c) Row 4: concrete is a made, designed mixture, while wood is natural

questions.q: A shop sign says: 'Stainless steel bottles - made of one pure element!' Using what the chapter says about stainless steel, show that the sign cannot be true.
questions.a: Stainless steel contains iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon, so it is made of more than one substance. An element is a pure substance made of identical atoms of one kind. A material made of four substances mixed together is a mixture (an alloy), so it cannot be one pure element, however uniform it looks.
s: stainless steel contains iron, nickel, chromium and carbon
an element has only one kind of identical atom
so stainless steel is a mixture (alloy), not an element

questions.q:
A school water purifier is labelled 'pure drinking water'. A lab finds that the water from it has a small amount of mineral salts dissolved in it.
(a) In which sense is the label 'pure' being used? Give the reason.
(b) Is the drinking water a compound, a mixture, or neither? Explain, using what the chapter says about water.
questions.a: (a) In the everyday sense: it is unadulterated, with nothing cheaper or harmful added. It is not pure in the scientific sense, because it contains other substances (the dissolved salts). (b) A mixture. Water itself is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen, but the drinking water contains this compound with salts dissolved in it, so as a whole it is a mixture of more than one substance.
s: (a) everyday sense; not scientifically pure, as salts are present
(b) a mixture: the compound water with dissolved salts

questions.q:
Ten items are found in and around a school: air, drinking water, an iron rod, an aluminium sheet, a stainless steel sink, a wooden door, a concrete slab, a steel beam, common salt and sugar.
(a) Sort all ten into elements, compounds and mixtures, and give how many are in each group. (3)
(b) The construction items in the list are the iron rod, aluminium sheet, wooden door, concrete slab and steel beam. Which group do most of them belong to, and what does this suggest about why engineers rely on their understanding of mixtures? (2)
questions.a: (a) Elements: iron rod, aluminium sheet (2). Compounds: drinking water, common salt, sugar (3). Mixtures: air, stainless steel sink, wooden door, concrete slab, steel beam (5). (b) Mixtures: three of the five construction items (wood, concrete, steel) are mixtures and two (iron, aluminium) are elements. Engineers and material scientists design mixtures to get materials with the properties a job needs, which single substances alone may not have.
s: (a) correct sorting: 2 elements, 3 compounds, 5 mixtures
(b) mixtures are the majority (3 of 5); mixtures are designed for useful properties

questions.q: A footbridge uses 120 tonnes of steel beams and 30 tonnes of aluminium panels (illustrative figures). What percentage of this metal, by mass, is a mixture?

Nisha's mineral-hunt notebook from a geology camp in Jharkhand has four entries. The lab results were given by her instructor.
Sample 1: shiny yellow nugget; lab: only gold atoms. Nisha wrote: 'native mineral, an element'.
Sample 2: clear glassy crystal; lab: silicon and oxygen combined in a fixed ratio. Nisha wrote: 'native mineral, an element'.
Sample 3: grey stone; under a magnifying glass, three different kinds of grain are seen. Nisha wrote: 'a mineral with a fixed composition'.
Sample 4: yellow lumps; lab: only sulfur atoms. Nisha wrote: 'a compound mineral'.
(a) Which entry is correct? Give the reason.
(b) Correct the entry for Sample 2.
(c) Correct the entry for Sample 3.
(d) Correct Sample 4, and then decide which of the four samples could give an element without any compound having to be broken down.
questions.a: (a) Sample 1: gold is a native mineral, a pure element and not a compound. (b) Sample 2 is a mineral that is a compound, made of more than one element (silicon and oxygen); it is not a native mineral. (c) Sample 3 is a rock, a mixture of minerals (the three kinds of grain), not a single mineral. (d) Sample 4 is a native mineral, the element sulfur, not a compound. Samples 1 and 4 are already pure elements, so they give gold and sulfur without breaking down any compound.
s: (a) Sample 1 correct: gold is a native mineral, an element
(b) Sample 2 is a compound mineral
(c) Sample 3 is a rock, a mixture of minerals
(d) Sample 4 is a native element; Samples 1 and 4 give elements directly

questions.q: The iron for a new bridge comes from a mineral that a lab shows is a compound of iron and oxygen. What must happen to get the iron?
questions.a: The compound must be broken down to extract it
o: The compound must be broken down to extract it
The iron grains can be picked out with a magnifier
Nothing, as the mineral is already pure iron
The iron can be filtered out after soaking the rock

questions.q: Under a magnifying glass, a rock from a hillside in Karnataka shows glassy grains, flaky shiny grains and dark green grains. What is the rock?
questions.a: A mixture of different minerals
o: A mixture of different minerals
One mineral with a fixed composition
A pure element, as it is natural
A compound, since it is a solid

questions.q: True or false? 'Sulfur found naturally in the Earth can be both a mineral and an element.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Minerals are natural, solid substances with a fixed chemical composition. Most are compounds, but some, the native minerals, are pure elements; sulfur is one of the non-metal native minerals, so natural sulfur is a mineral and also an element.
s: verdict: true
native minerals are pure elements, and sulfur is a native mineral

questions.q: From the list quartz, calcite, mica, gold, sulfur, a granite-like rock and a concrete block, the number of items that are minerals which are compounds is ___.

Assertion (A): A granite-like rock is not called a mineral, even though it is natural and solid.
Reason (R): Most rocks are a mixture of minerals.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Write a short situation of three or four sentences, set in your home or school, that shows how an everyday product depends on minerals. Use either cement or talcum powder, and name the mineral or minerals it comes from.
questions.a: Any correct situation, for example: Our school is building a new classroom, and the masons mix cement with sand and water. The cement was made in a factory from calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide, which are minerals or are obtained from minerals. Without these minerals dug from the Earth, there would be no cement for the walls. (Or: talcum powder used after a bath is made from the mineral talc.)
s: a realistic everyday setting using cement or talcum powder
the correct mineral source named
the dependence on minerals made clear

questions.q:
(a) Cement is made from calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide. Is cement itself a single mineral? Give the reason.
(b) Explain why a cement factory depends on minerals.
questions.a: (a) No. Cement is made by people from four different substances; a mineral is a single natural, solid substance found on the Earth with a fixed chemical composition. (b) Each of the four substances cement is made from (calcite, quartz, alumina, iron oxide) is a mineral or is obtained from minerals, so without minerals the factory would have nothing to make cement from.
s: (a) no: made by people from several substances, not one natural substance
(b) all its ingredients are minerals or come from minerals

questions.q: Samples of the mineral calcite are collected from a quarry in Rajasthan and from another in Gujarat. What does the chapter lead you to expect when both are analysed?
questions.a: The same chemical composition in both
o: The same chemical composition in both
A different composition, as the places differ
One a compound and the other an element
Both to be mixtures of many minerals

questions.q: Kabir says, 'A rock and a mineral are the same thing; quartz is just a kind of rock.' Do you agree? Explain what each term means.
questions.a: No. Most rocks are a mixture of minerals, whose grains can often be seen with the eyes, a magnifying glass or a microscope. A mineral is a natural, solid substance with a fixed chemical composition, usually a compound and rarely a pure element. Quartz is a mineral (a compound), one of the substances that rocks are made of, not a rock itself.
s: verdict: disagree
a rock is usually a mixture of minerals
a mineral is a natural solid of fixed composition; quartz is a mineral

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: A native mineral of carbon is a pure element.
Statement 2: Cement is made from substances that are minerals or are obtained from minerals.
Statement 3: Every mineral is a compound made of more than one element.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

2 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
A collector has 10 mineral specimens. A lab finds that 4 contain only one kind of atom each, and 6 contain atoms of two or more elements combined in a fixed ratio.
(a) How many of the specimens are native minerals? Give the reason.
(b) She finds an eleventh lump that shows three different kinds of grain under a magnifying glass. Can it join either of her two groups? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 4. A native mineral is a pure element, made of one kind of atom; the other 6 are compound minerals. (b) No. A lump with three kinds of grain is a rock, a mixture of minerals, not a single mineral; it is neither a native mineral nor a compound mineral.
s: (a) 4, as native minerals are pure elements
(b) no: it is a rock, a mixture of minerals

questions.q:
Match each lab result with what the sample is.
Column A:
1. Found naturally; made only of copper atoms
2. A natural crystal of calcium, carbon and oxygen combined in a fixed ratio
3. A stone showing flaky shiny grains and glassy grains
4. A white powder made in a factory from talc
Column B:
a. A rock, a mixture of minerals
b. A product made from a mineral
c. A native mineral
d. A mineral that is a compound

'Minerals are most often compounds, but rarely they can be pure elements.' A museum in Bhubaneswar displays eight minerals: quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene, olivine, gold, silver and sulfur.
(a) Sort the eight into native minerals (elements) and compound minerals. (2)
(b) What fraction of the display is native minerals? (1)
(c) A visitor says the display shows that native minerals are not rare at all. Explain whether the display can be used to judge how common native minerals are, and how the statement in quotation marks should be understood. (2)
questions.a: (a) Native minerals (elements): gold, silver, sulfur. Compound minerals: quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene, olivine. (b) 3 out of 8 (3/8). (c) No. A museum chooses its specimens to show different kinds of mineral, so it puts native minerals on display on purpose; its share does not show how often they occur. The statement is about minerals in general on Earth: most minerals are compounds made of more than one element, and only a few, the native minerals, are pure elements.
s: (a) gold, silver, sulfur native; the other five compounds
(c) a chosen display cannot show how common they are; the statement is about minerals on Earth in general

questions.q: A lab reports that a mineral sample is made only of silicon atoms and oxygen atoms, combined in a fixed ratio. How should the sample be classified?
questions.a: A compound mineral
o: A compound mineral
A native mineral
A rock, a mixture of minerals
An element, since it is natural

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'Talcum powder and cement each come straight from just one mineral.' Which correction is right?
questions.a: Talc alone gives talcum powder; cement needs several
o: Talc alone gives talcum powder; cement needs several
Cement comes from calcite alone; talcum powder needs several
Both are made from calcite, quartz and alumina together
Neither of them depends on minerals in any way

questions.q:
(a) The chapter says many things we use are made from minerals, or from elements extracted from minerals. Give one example of each kind from the chapter.
(b) Explain why an element usually has to be 'extracted' from a mineral, but not from a native mineral.
questions.a: (a) Made from a mineral: talcum powder, from the mineral talc (or cement from calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide). From elements extracted from minerals: metals, which are obtained from minerals. (b) Most minerals are compounds, in which the element is combined with other elements, so it must be got out of the compound. A native mineral is already the pure element, such as gold or copper, so there is nothing to extract it from.
s: (a) one product made from a mineral and one from extracted elements (metals)
(b) most minerals are compounds; a native mineral is already the element

questions.q: Asif says, 'Copper found in the ground as a native mineral is an element, but the copper wire made from it is not a mineral.' Is he right? Explain both halves.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. Native copper is a native mineral: a mineral that is a pure element, so it is both a mineral and an element. A mineral is a natural, solid substance found on the Earth; copper wire is a manufactured object, so although it is still made of the element copper, it is not a mineral.
s: verdict: right
native copper is a mineral and a pure element
minerals are natural substances found on Earth, so the made wire is not one

questions.q:
(a) Give the features the chapter uses to describe a mineral.
(b) Explain why stainless steel, though solid and the same all through, is not a mineral.
questions.a: (a) A mineral is a natural, solid substance found on the Earth, with a fixed chemical composition; most often a compound, rarely a pure element. (b) Stainless steel is not natural: people make it by mixing iron, nickel, chromium and a small amount of carbon. It is an alloy, a mixture, not a single natural substance with a fixed composition.
s: (a) natural, solid, found on Earth, fixed composition
(b) stainless steel is a man-made mixture, not natural

questions.q:
A district wants to start factories. A survey (illustrative) finds three deposits: Hill P has calcite and quartz; Hill Q has talc; Valley R has iron oxide and alumina. A cement plant needs calcite, quartz, alumina and iron oxide. A talcum powder unit needs only talc. This year the district can build a road to only ONE of the three sites, and nothing can be brought in from outside the district.
(a) Which product depends on a single mineral?
(b) Which sites would the cement plant need, and why?
(c) Explain whether cement itself is a mineral.
(d) Decide which site the one road should go to so that a factory can start this year, and justify using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Talcum powder: it is made from the mineral talc alone. (b) Both Hill P (calcite, quartz) and Valley R (iron oxide, alumina), because cement needs all four, and no single site has them all. (c) No. Cement is made by people from several minerals or substances obtained from minerals; a mineral is a single natural, solid substance found on the Earth. (d) Hill Q. With one road, the cement plant cannot get all four of its materials (it needs both P and R), but the talcum powder unit needs only talc, which Hill Q supplies.
s: (a) talcum powder, from talc only

questions.q:
Compare four items: a gold nugget found in a river, a quartz crystal, a grey rock made of several kinds of mineral grain, and a concrete block.
(a) For each, say whether it is a mineral or not, and whether it is an element, a compound or a mixture. (2)
(b) The rock and the concrete are both mixtures. Explain the difference between them that decides which is natural. (1)
(c) Which one item could give a metal without any compound being broken down? Explain why the quartz crystal could not give an element in the same way. (2)
questions.a: (a) Gold nugget: a mineral (native mineral), an element. Quartz crystal: a mineral, a compound. Grey rock: not a single mineral; a mixture of minerals. Concrete block: not a mineral; a mixture (the chapter names concrete as a mixture used for building). (b) The rock is formed in nature as a mixture of minerals; concrete is made by people. (c) The gold nugget: it is already the pure element gold, a native mineral. Quartz is a compound mineral: its elements are combined, so an element would have to be extracted from it by breaking the compound down; only a native mineral is already the element itself.
s: (a) gold mineral/element; quartz mineral/compound; rock mixture of minerals; concrete mixture, not a mineral
(b) the rock forms naturally; concrete is made by people
(c) the gold nugget, as a native element; compound minerals need extraction
